Coinholder polls count one ZEC as one vote at a snapshot height, and coins may be moved right after the snapshot. This ZIP changes only the weighting: a ballot’s weight rises linearly with how long its coins stay locked past the snapshot, up to a cap of one halving interval; unlocked coins keep a small floor weight. One evidence class works today: transparent outputs locked with

. A second class for shielded locks is reserved for a consensus ZIP. Quorum and the ZIP 1016 participation threshold stay in unweighted ZEC. The transparent class reveals the voter’s output, amount, and unlock height on chain, which the current shielded polling path does not; the shielded class is the intended end state.
Coinholder polling gives holders a voice alongside developers, users, and miners. ZIP 1016
makes it the deciding input for the Coinholder-Controlled Fund, and about 2.4 million of 3.6 million eligible ZEC voted in the NU7 scope poll of September 2026
The status quo is one ZEC, one vote, at a snapshot, with coins movable the moment the snapshot passes

. Someone who buys the week of the vote and sells the week after is not a holder; they are renting a vote. This ZIP favours people credibly in it for the long haul. Someone willing to lock ZEC for years should have a big say, not the only say. A whale who locks for years still gets a big vote; they have put their coins where their vote is. The change removes the cheap vote, not the big one.
There is no timelock for shielded notes. Transparent outputs can be locked with
, which Zebra enforces on every transparent input
. Sapling, Orchard, and Ironwood notes have no script and no lock field, and a transaction’s
is ignored when no transparent input has a non-final sequence number
, so it cannot lock a shielded-only spend. Three options were considered:
A process-only ZIP using transparent locks. It works at the protocol level, not the tooling level: the live mechanism accepts only notes in the
. It asks holders to unshield for full weight, which is at odds with the point of Zcash. Not acceptable as the only option.

A consensus ZIP adding a lock to shielded notes. The smallest version is a lock-height field in the Ironwood note commitment, one circuit constraint, and one consensus rule (see [Class S]). That is a new circuit version for a pool created, with formal verification, after the Orchard soundness vulnerability
. It is not small and needs a network upgrade.
Two ZIPs: this process ZIP, defining weighting over any lock the protocol can prove, with the transparent class as an interim, plus a later consensus ZIP for shielded locks.
Option 3 is chosen. Everything below is defined over lock records, so the shielded class can be added without rewriting this ZIP.
Under the live mechanism, validators learn neither who voted nor how much ZEC a ballot carried; amounts are encrypted and only totals are decrypted

. A ballot under [Class T] reveals an output, its value, and its unlock height on chain to everyone, and links the ballot to that output unless the operator encrypts ballot contents. A voter who unshields to lock also reveals the unshielding transaction. That cost is why Class S is the intended end state.

The shielded class is required to reveal no more than the current shielded path: the lock length stays a private witness, the multiplier is applied inside the proof, and locked notes are indistinguishable from unlocked notes on chain, including when spent.
A ballot’s weight depends on both the amount of ZEC and how long it is locked past the snapshot.
Borrowing, hedging, or splitting to gain weight costs more than under amount-only weighting.
Weighting is defined over an abstract lock record, so shielded locks can be added without changing the rules.
The shielded class reveals no more than the current shielded polling path.
Coins with no holder, such as protocol-level lockboxes, cannot be voted.
This ZIP does not change who is eligible to vote, what polls are held, or what polls decide. It changes weighting only.
It does not propose on-chain binding governance. Polls remain what ZIP 1016 says they are.
It does not change mining, block subsidy, or funding streams.

Class S, shielded locks, is reserved for a consensus ZIP. That ZIP MUST provide: a way to fix an unlock height at note creation that consensus enforces on spends; a proof usable within the operator’s shielded path that yields a lock record for notes unspent at
, with the multiplier applied inside the proof; and locked notes indistinguishable from unlocked notes on chain, including when spent.

The smallest design known: a lock-height field inside the Ironwood note commitment (zero for none); a circuit constraint that the field is at most a per-bundle minimum height; a consensus rule that a transaction with a non-zero minimum height is invalid in any block below it; and wallets that set that value on every transaction so locked spends do not stand out.

A custodian that owes coins on demand cannot lock them without a liquidity mismatch, so voting customer coins at full weight gets harder. That is intended. The limits: a custodian can lock its own float or accept the mismatch, and this ZIP does not verify custody.

Rationale for the cap and floor
The cap is one halving interval: the longest horizon over which the protocol itself plans issuance, and the four-year maximum of vote-escrow systems

. The floor is non-zero so that this ZIP does not change who can vote; zero would exclude every shielded holder until Class S exists. One tenth is the weight of an unlocked vote in Polkadot’s conviction voting
